text: Arrays handle lists. Objects handle structure - a single thing, like one incident, with several named pieces of information attached to it. This lesson covers building objects, reading their properties two different ways, and nesting them.

An object literal is written in curly braces, as a set of key-value pairs. This incident object has four properties: number, priority, shortDescription, and isEscalated. Unlike an array, you never access a property by position - you always access it by its name.

Most of the time you'll read a property with dot notation - incident dot number. Bracket notation does the same thing but takes the property name as a string, and that opens up something dot notation can't do: if the property name itself is stored in a variable, like fieldName holding the word priority, bracket notation can look it up at runtime. Dot notation has no way to do that - it only works with a literal name typed directly into the code.

A property's value can itself be another object. Here, assignedTo holds its own object with a name and an email. To reach a deeply nested value, you chain dot notation step by step - incident dot assignedTo dot name first gets the assignedTo object, then gets name from inside it.

This matters directly for where the course is headed. Starting next chapter, GlideRecord gives you fields on a real ServiceNow record, and later lessons work with JSON data from REST calls - both are shaped exactly like these nested objects. Getting comfortable with plain object properties now, with no ServiceNow involved yet, is what makes that material click instead of feeling unfamiliar.

Key-value properties, two ways to access them, and nesting to represent real structure. Next up: the Fundamentals Lab, where you'll put variables, functions, arrays, and objects to work together in one real scenario.
